interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between bandwidth and latency, and why do people confuse them?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd define both crisply first: bandwidth is capacity — bits per second a link can carry; latency is delay — the time for one bit to make the trip. They're independent: you can have high bandwidth and high latency (a satellite link) or low bandwidth and low latency (a short DSL hop).

People confuse them because in casual use "slow internet" describes both symptoms — a slow download (bandwidth-bound) and laggy video calls (latency-bound) both feel like "slow internet," but they need different fixes. Upgrading bandwidth doesn't touch physical propagation delay, so it won't fix a laggy call to a far-away server.

**Testing:** whether you can name the actual mechanism (propagation vs throughput) instead of treating "slow" as one undifferentiated complaint.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Bandwidth vs latency

interviewQuestions.question: Why does the internet use packet switching instead of circuit switching?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd frame it as an efficiency-vs-guarantee trade-off. Circuit switching reserves fixed capacity for a whole session, which wastes idle time; packet switching lets many flows statistically share the same links, so idle moments from one flow get used by another — far cheaper to scale to millions of bursty, mostly-idle connections like web browsing.

The cost is no hard per-flow guarantee: under load, packets queue and delay becomes variable. That's an acceptable trade for most traffic (web, email, most video), which is why the internet standardized on it; it's a bad trade for things needing a hard guarantee, which is part of why legacy telephony kept circuit switching for so long.

**Testing:** whether you understand this as a deliberate efficiency trade-off, not "packet switching is strictly better."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why packet switching won
